description: We’re a team of engineering students passionate about AI/ML, software, data visualization, and space technology. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we’re building an intuitive tool to compare Moon South Pole landing sites, sunlight, and communication windows. We’re looking for curious teammates skilled in development, UI/UX, AI/ML, astronomy, GIS, or research.
summary:
At the Moon's south pole the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon, and Earth hangs low too. A ridge a few kilometres away can put a lander in shadow, or cut it off from Earth, for days. A landing site is only half the answer: the other half is the date.

Luna Atlas is a live web app that answers both. Pick a site and a mission length, and it tells you whether you can land, when the next landing window opens, and which date in the next year gives the most sunlight or the most Earth contact. It shows why: you can stand on the site in 3D and watch the real Sun and Earth move over the real horizon. Every answer is computed live from NASA/JPL ephemerides and NASA LRO laser-altimeter terrain, and every scientific check behind it is shown in the app, including the ones that failed.
details:
Luna Atlas is a web app for picking a landing site and a landing date at the Moon's south pole. You choose a site and a date, and it tells you if you can land, when the next landing window is, where the Sun and Earth are compared to the local horizon, and how long until sunset and Earthset. It also gives the sunlight on a solar panel (before panel efficiency), the best landing dates over the next year, a side-by-side compare of sites, and a "Launch slipped?" button that finds the next window if the launch moves by a week, a month or three months.

The reason this is hard at the pole is that the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon. So whether a site gets sunlight depends mostly on the hills around it, not on latitude. Same for Earth, which also sits low and moves up and down a little over the month. A lander needs both, sunlight for power and Earth in view to talk to the team, so you have to compute the horizon properly.

How it works. We use NASA/JPL SPICE kernels (DE421 plus the lunar orientation kernels) to get the Sun and Earth direction from any point on the Moon at any time. For the horizon we use NASA LOLA terrain: 5 m per pixel at two south-pole sites and 240 m per pixel for everything from 60°S to the pole. For each site we trace the horizon in 720 directions out to 200 km. Then we find when the Sun and Earth cross that horizon (to 10 s) and check five landing rules, like Sun up at touchdown, enough sunlight after it and Earth in view. The rules are our choices based on Apollo and recent landers, and the app shows them. Horizons are cached on the server so repeat answers are fast. North of 60°S we have no terrain map loaded, so it uses a flat horizon there and says so on the answer.

Testing. Before each test we wrote down what would count as a pass, and we kept the failures in the results. Our Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.041 arcseconds. We checked 7 real landings and 6 passed. Blue Ghost 1 failed, its sunset was 2.4 hours off, because its site is north of our terrain map and the flat horizon is not good enough there. We compared our shadows with 6 NASA LRO camera photos of the pole and 5 matched. We also compared against NASA Goddard sunlight and slope maps. All of this is on the Evidence screen in the app.

Things we found. When we ran published landing points through the terrain, some results surprised us. The published point for Malapert Massif is on the side of the mountain facing away from Earth, so Earth is never visible there and it never passes our landing check. The top of the ridge 10.7 km east sees Earth 70% of the month and the Sun 84%, so we added a button to try that point. LOLA Site 004's published point gets 0% sunlight in January 2027, but points 100 m away get 96 to 100%. It sits in a small dip about 7 m deep, and we are not sure yet if the dip is real or comes from gaps in the terrain data. The Shackleton reference point we used turned out to be on the inner wall of the crater. We also saw that terrain resolution matters a lot: Site 001 gets 69% sunlight on the 5 m map and 100% on the 240 m map for the same month.

What it does not do. It is not a landing safety check, because rocks smaller than about 10 m are below what the terrain shows. Earth in view means line of sight, not a confirmed radio link. The panel numbers are sunlight before panel efficiency, not power output, and the battery in the 3D view is only illustrative.

Built with Python (FastAPI, SpiceyPy, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj) for all the calculations, and React with three.js for the 3D Moon. It runs in Docker on a cloud server, with tests in pytest and vitest. No special hardware. We used Claude as a coding assistant; the numbers come from our code running on NASA data and are checked against the NASA sources above.

Who it is for: CLPS mission planners who want a quick first answer, and students or anyone who wants to see why landing at the pole is hard. There is a short guided tour, every view can be shared as a link, and it works on phones.
